conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Dr. Ramirez—I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician, which simply means I specialize in the emotional well-being of new mothers.  

To get a quick, caring snapshot of how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, I’ll be using a short questionnaire called the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s just 10 gentle questions about the past week, and it helps us see if you might benefit from extra support or resources.  

Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words; there are no right or wrong answers.  

Ready to begin?  

First, how have you been feeling in general over the past seven days—have you been able to enjoy things, or has joy felt hard to reach lately?

*shifts a little in the chair, clasping my hands in my lap*

To be honest...most things feel kind of flat. Like, yesterday my sister came over and brought those lemon bars I used to love, and I ate one because I thought “maybe this will feel nice,” but it tasted like nothing special. I still go through the motions—snuggling the baby, watching a show, texting friends—but the spark I used to get from those things just isn’t really there. It’s like I’m doing them more because I “should” than because they make me happy. I can still laugh once in a while—like when the baby makes those funny milk-drunk faces—but the joy fades fast and I’m back to feeling blah or just...empty.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*offers a small, tired smile*

Yeah...I do still laugh sometimes. Like, my husband will do something goofy while he’s changing her diaper and I’ll catch myself giggling—but then the laugh kind of fizzles out and I feel flat again. It’s not like before, when a good joke or funny show would keep me cheerful for a while. Now the laughter feels short, almost like it’s happening to someone else.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*eyes drop to my lap*

Not really. I keep telling myself I should be excited about little things—like my mom’s coming over this weekend and we’re supposed to go pick out a bigger onesie for the baby—but when I think about it I just feel… nothing. Or I worry it’ll be too much work to get us both ready. Most mornings I open my eyes and think, “What’s even the point today?” I still plan stuff, but it’s more because I don’t want to let people down than because I’m actually looking forward to anything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*nods slowly, pressing my lips together*

Yeah... I do that a lot. Yesterday she was fussy for almost two hours and I kept thinking, "It must be something I ate," or, "I probably didn’t burp her long enough." When she finally spit up a ton, my first thought was, "Great, I over-fed her—I'm already messing this up." Even little stuff like forgetting to bring a spare onesie when we went to the clinic makes me feel like the worst mom. My brain keeps telling me I should know better, that a "good" mother would have it all figured out by now.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*wrings the edge of my sweater*

All the time. Like, I’ll be feeding her and suddenly imagine she’s going to choke on the tiniest drip of milk, so I sit her straight up and pat her back even though she’s fine. At night I’ll stare at the monitor watching her chest rise and fall, and if it looks even a little off my heart starts racing. Yesterday I burst into tears because I couldn’t find the nasal aspirator—convinced she’d stop breathing and I wouldn’t be ready. I know the worries aren’t logical, but I can’t shut them off; they just loop over and over until I feel shaky and sick to my stomach.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*nods, voice a little shaky*

Yeah... it hits out of nowhere. Like, I'll be folding her tiny socks and suddenly my heart's racing and I feel like I can't breathe—like something awful is about to happen, but I couldn't tell you what. A few nights ago I was rocking her in the nursery and I had to grip the chair because the room felt like it was closing in. I kept thinking, "What if I drop her? What if I pass out and no one's here?" It passes after a minute or two, but in that moment I'm frozen, terrified, and I have no idea why.
Things have been getting on top of me

*nods, exhaling slowly*

Most days, yeah. It feels like I’m drowning in small stuff—dishes pile up, the diaper pail overflows, texts go unanswered, and each thing seems huge. I’ll start one chore, hear the baby cry, rush to her, then completely forget what I was doing. By noon I’m exhausted and the house is still a mess. Sometimes I just sit on the couch staring at the clutter, heart racing, thinking, “How is everyone else managing?” I manage to keep her fed and changed, but everything else feels like too much. I end up snapping at my partner over nothing, then feel awful about it.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*twists the fabric of my sweatpants*

Yeah... once she finally settles around ten, I lie there staring at the ceiling for hours. My mind just keeps spinning—replaying every little thing I did wrong, worrying about her next feeding, wondering if I’m cut out for this. Some nights I finally drift off only to jolt awake, heart pounding, convinced I heard her cry when she’s still asleep. Even when I do sleep it’s light and restless. By morning I feel like I’ve run a marathon, but I still have to get up and do it all again.
I have felt sad or miserable

*eyes well up a little, voice dropping*

Pretty much every day. It’s like this heavy blanket I can’t shake off. I’ll be changing her diaper and suddenly feel tears coming for no clear reason—just this wave of sadness that sits on my chest. I look at her tiny face and instead of feeling only love, I feel guilt and this ache I can’t name. Sometimes I cry in the shower so no one sees. I keep waiting for the “happy mom” feeling everyone talks about, but most of the time I just feel... empty and alone, even when people are right here.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*eyes sting, voice cracks*

Yeah... it kind of leaks out whether I want it to or not. Yesterday I was just mixing formula and the spoon clinked the bottle harder than usual, and suddenly I was sobbing over the sink. I tried to stop because I didn’t want her to hear, but I couldn’t. It happens maybe once or twice a week—this wave hits and I end up crying in the nursery with the door shut, telling myself to get it together before someone sees. I feel ridiculous, but the tears just come and I can’t shut them off.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*nods slowly, not meeting your eyes*

A couple times this week... nothing planned or anything. It'll just flash through—like when I'm rocking her at 3 a.m. and feel totally useless, I'll think, "She'd be better off if I weren't here." I picture the medicine cabinet or driving off the road for a second, then shove it away and hold her tighter. I haven't told anyone because it scares me, and I know I wouldn't actually do it... but yeah, the thought's been there, drifting in and out.

You've shared how the last weeks have felt heavy: joy seems out of reach, daily tasks feel overwhelming, and worries about your baby loop constantly in your mind. Nights are long, with restless sleep and tears that arrive without warning, while moments of laughter fade quickly. You described feeling guilty for small mishaps and, at times, fleeting thoughts that your daughter might be better off without you.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Laughs rarely and fleetingly; joy markedly diminished and detached, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports anhedonia, feeling "nothing" and "what's even the point today?", matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame for routine infant issues (feeding, spitting, forgetting items), indicating it happens "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive worries about infant safety that are overwhelming and looping, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes with physical symptoms (racing heart, breathlessness, room closing in) and safety fears, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to manage routine tasks, racing heart, and snapping at partner, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to persistent worry and rumination, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>"Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, uncontrollable crying episodes occurring weekly, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intrusive thoughts of self-harm occurring several times this week, matching "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS responses show high scores (27/30) across depressive and anxiety items, meeting threshold for probable <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Patient reports daily <sym>low mood</sym>, <sym>loss of interest</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, <sym>feelings of inadequacy</sym>, and <sym>passive suicidal ideation</sym> several times this week, aligning with <med>DSM-5</med> criteria. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Contact your <med>primary care provider</med> or obstetrician today for urgent evaluation
2. Ask about same-day referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> or psychiatrist
3. Call a 24/7 crisis line if thoughts of self-harm intensify: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
4. Arrange practical support overnight (partner, family, postpartum doula) to allow 4-5 hour stretches of sleep
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 1-2 weeks to monitor progress
6. Begin gentle daily routine: short outdoor walk, balanced meals, hydration, 5-minute breathing breaks
7. Discuss medication options compatible with breastfeeding if recommended by prescriber
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 2–3 wks post-delivery, primiparous, breastfeeding, partner present.

Responses to EPDS-equivalent items:

1. Anhedonia: laughs briefly, no sustained pleasure (endorsed)  
2. Loss of interest / “nothing to look forward to” (endorsed)  
3. Excessive guilt / self-blame re infant care (endorsed)  
4. Free-floating anxiety, catastrophic worries (endorsed)  
5. Panic symptoms without clear trigger (endorsed)  
6. Feeling overwhelmed / unable to cope with daily tasks (endorsed)  
7. Mood-related insomnia (sleep onset & maintenance) (endorsed)  
8. Persistent sadness, emotional numbness (endorsed)  
9. Frequent crying spells (endorsed)  
10. Passive suicidal ideation (“she’d be better off if I weren’t here”) twice this week; no plan, no intent stated (endorsed)

Pattern: High endorsement across core depressive (items 1,2,7,8,9) and anxiety (4,5) domains; prominent guilt, anhedonia, panic, functional overload, and passive SI.

Safety: Positive for passive suicidal ideation; no protective factors elicited.

Risk factors: First-time mother, sleep deprivation, self-criticism, social comparison, intrusive harm worries.

Screening impression: Meets clinical threshold for probable moderate-to-severe postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; immediate safety assessment and follow-up indicated.
